title: Chronic Kidney Disease: Stage by eGFR and Albuminuria, Then Slow Progression
bottomLine: CKD requires chronic kidney abnormality, not one low eGFR. Confirm chronicity, stage by GFR and albuminuria, identify cause and progression risk, treat blood pressure/diabetes/cardiorenal risk, avoid nephrotoxins and refer according to kidney-failure risk, rapid progression or diagnostic uncertainty.
recognize: CKD may be present with reduced eGFR, persistent albuminuria or other structural/urinary abnormalities for at least the chronicity interval.
Albuminuria independently predicts kidney and cardiovascular risk and changes treatment intensity.
differentiate: AKI/AKD can temporarily lower eGFR and should not be labelled CKD without evidence of chronicity.
Heavy proteinuria, active sediment, systemic disease or rapid decline may indicate a glomerular or other specific disease rather than nonspecific CKD.
assessment: Review BP, diabetes, vascular disease, NSAIDs/OTC/herbal exposure, family history, urinary symptoms, volume status and prior creatinine/ACR trajectory.
workup: Use serum creatinine/eGFR and urine ACR, repeat abnormal results to establish chronicity, and add urinalysis/imaging/cause-directed serology when the phenotype warrants it.
Use validated kidney-failure risk prediction in appropriate CKD stages to guide referral/planning.
management: Control BP and diabetes, use RAAS blockade for appropriate albuminuric disease and SGLT2-based kidney protection when indicated, manage lipids/smoking and avoid nephrotoxins.
Prepare for kidney replacement or conservative care early enough when progression risk is high; dialysis is not started solely because eGFR crosses one outpatient number.
medicationSafety: Review every medication for renal dosing and nephrotoxicity; NSAIDs can worsen kidney function, BP and volume status.
A modest expected creatinine change after RAAS/SGLT2 initiation is interpreted in context rather than causing reflex discontinuation, while severe rise/hyperkalemia requires reassessment.
counselling: Teach sick-day/nephrotoxin precautions where appropriate, BP/diabetes self-management and why urine albumin matters even when the patient feels well.
followUp: Trend eGFR and ACR at frequency matched to risk and close the loop on nephrology referral when criteria are met.
examTrap: Diagnosing CKD from one creatinine during an acute illness or starting dialysis solely from an eGFR value without clinical indications.
oneLinePearl: CKD is chronicity + GFR + albuminuria + cause—not one creatinine.

title: Acute Kidney Injury: Find the Cause and Treat the Complications
bottomLine: AKI is an acute change in kidney function detected by creatinine trend and/or urine output. Stabilize life-threatening potassium, acid-base or volume complications while classifying the cause as perfusion-related, intrinsic renal or obstructive; do not rely on eGFR as if kidney function were at steady state during rapidly changing creatinine.
recognize: Oliguria, rising creatinine, volume overload, hyperkalemia or acidosis may occur, but nonoliguric AKI is common.
Sepsis, hypovolemia, nephrotoxins, contrast, urinary obstruction and glomerular/interstitial disease are important causes.
differentiate: Pre-renal physiology can progress to tubular injury if prolonged; obstruction can be bilateral or affect a solitary functioning kidney.
A bland urinalysis does not exclude significant AKI, while active sediment can point toward glomerular/interstitial disease.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, volume status, sepsis, urine output, bladder retention, recent procedures/contrast, NSAIDs/RAAS/diuretics/antibiotics and baseline renal function.
workup: Trend creatinine/electrolytes/urine output, perform urinalysis/microscopy when useful and use bladder scan/renal ultrasound for obstruction risk.
Order cause-directed serology or imaging for suspected glomerular, vascular or interstitial disease.
management: Restore perfusion when deficient, stop/adjust nephrotoxins, treat sepsis/obstruction and manage potassium, acidosis and pulmonary edema.
Dialysis is complication/clinical-indication driven rather than a creatinine threshold alone.
medicationSafety: Hold or dose-adjust renally cleared/nephrotoxic medications as clinically appropriate and reassess before restarting after recovery.
Avoid reflex large fluid boluses in already congested/cardiorenal patients.
counselling: After recovery, review nephrotoxin exposure and explain that kidney function should be rechecked because AKI increases future CKD risk.
followUp: Document baseline/recovery creatinine, medication restart plan and post-AKI kidney monitoring.
examTrap: Using calculated eGFR as a stable measure during rapidly evolving AKI or starting dialysis solely because creatinine is high.
oneLinePearl: In AKI, trend and complications matter more than a single creatinine.

title: Proteinuria: Quantify Albumin, Confirm Persistence, Find the Kidney Disease
bottomLine: Proteinuria is a kidney-risk marker and a diagnostic clue. Use urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio for most CKD risk assessment, confirm persistence outside transient illness/exercise/UTI, quantify severity and identify when heavy proteinuria or active sediment requires nephrology/glomerular evaluation.
recognize: Albuminuria can precede eGFR decline in diabetes/hypertension.
Marked proteinuria with edema, hypoalbuminemia or lipid abnormalities suggests nephrotic physiology.
differentiate: Transient proteinuria can occur with fever, strenuous exercise or infection.
Non-albumin protein can occur in plasma-cell disease and may be missed by albumin-specific testing.
assessment: Review diabetes, BP, edema, systemic autoimmune symptoms, infections, medications, pregnancy and family history.
workup: Use urine ACR and repeat to confirm chronicity; urinalysis/microscopy, renal function and targeted serology/protein studies depend on severity and associated findings.
Avoid relying on dipstick alone to quantify kidney risk.
management: Treat the cause and optimize BP/diabetes/cardiorenal therapy, including RAAS/SGLT2 strategies when indicated.
Refer heavy/nephrotic proteinuria, active sediment, rapid eGFR decline or uncertain cause.
medicationSafety: RAAS blockade and nsMRA therapy require potassium/renal monitoring.
Avoid dual ACE inhibitor plus ARB therapy solely to reduce albuminuria.
counselling: Explain that urine albumin predicts kidney and cardiovascular risk even when there are no urinary symptoms.
followUp: Trend ACR and eGFR after therapy changes at clinically appropriate intervals.
examTrap: Calling one positive dipstick chronic proteinuric kidney disease without quantification or confirmation.
oneLinePearl: Protein on dipstick is a clue; persistent quantified albuminuria is the risk signal.

title: Hematuria: Glomerular, Urologic, or Transient?
bottomLine: Hematuria requires confirmation and risk stratification. Separate glomerular clues such as proteinuria, dysmorphic cells/casts or renal dysfunction from urologic bleeding, infection, stones, exercise/menstrual contamination and malignancy risk; anticoagulation does not eliminate the need to investigate otherwise unexplained hematuria.
recognize: Gross visible hematuria has higher urologic malignancy significance than a single trace dipstick result.
Proteinuria, hypertension, renal dysfunction or casts suggest a renal/glomerular source.
differentiate: Dipstick detects heme and can be positive with hemoglobin/myoglobin without RBCs.
UTI-associated hematuria should resolve after infection treatment; persistent hematuria still requires appropriate evaluation.
assessment: Ask visible vs microscopic blood, pain, dysuria, stones, smoking, occupational exposure, anticoagulants, exercise, menstruation, trauma and systemic renal symptoms.
workup: Confirm microscopic hematuria with microscopy and repeat when transient contamination is plausible.
Use renal function/ACR and risk-based imaging/cystoscopy or nephrology workup based on glomerular versus urologic risk.
management: Treat infection/stone or other identified cause, but ensure persistent or high-risk hematuria reaches urology/nephrology as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not dismiss hematuria as 'from anticoagulation' without evaluating underlying pathology when indicated.
counselling: Explain why visible blood or persistent microscopic blood may need evaluation even when symptoms resolve.
followUp: Confirm resolution after transient causes and track referrals/results to diagnostic closure.
examTrap: Blaming persistent hematuria on warfarin and skipping malignancy or glomerular evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Hematuria has a source; anticoagulation may reveal it but does not explain it away.

title: Urinary Tract Infection: Treat the Syndrome, Not the Culture
bottomLine: Diagnose UTI from compatible urinary/systemic symptoms plus testing when indicated. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is generally not treated except defined situations such as pregnancy or selected urologic procedures; cloudy urine, odor or a positive culture alone is not a reason for antibiotics.
recognize: Cystitis commonly causes dysuria, frequency/urgency and suprapubic discomfort without systemic illness.
Fever, flank pain, vomiting or sepsis features move toward pyelonephritis/complicated infection.
differentiate: Vaginitis/STI can cause dysuria; asymptomatic bacteriuria/colonization is common in older/catheterized patients.
Delirium alone with a positive urine culture does not establish symptomatic UTI without compatible urinary/systemic evidence.
assessment: Assess urinary symptoms, fever/flank pain, pregnancy, sexual/STI context, catheter/anatomic disease, renal function, prior cultures/resistance and antibiotic exposure.
workup: Urinalysis and culture are used selectively based on presentation, recurrence/complication risk and pregnancy; culture is important for pyelonephritis/complicated/recurrent disease.
Avoid surveillance cultures in asymptomatic nonpregnant patients unless specifically indicated.
management: Use the narrowest effective antimicrobial and evidence-supported duration based on syndrome, pregnancy, renal function, allergies and local resistance.
Address obstruction/catheter issues and recurrent-UTI prevention individually.
medicationSafety: Renal function and pregnancy alter antibiotic selection/dose.
Avoid treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in most nonpregnant adults because harms/resistance outweigh benefit.
counselling: Explain why a positive culture without symptoms usually does not need antibiotics and give pyelonephritis return precautions.
followUp: Review culture when obtained and reassess recurrent infections for anatomic/behavioural contributors.
examTrap: Treating a positive urine culture in an asymptomatic older adult solely because they are confused.
oneLinePearl: Urine can contain bacteria without a UTI; treat symptoms and syndrome, not colonization.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association recurrent UTI resources

title: Pyelonephritis: Upper-Tract Infection, Severity, and Obstruction Risk
bottomLine: Pyelonephritis is upper-tract infection characterized by systemic illness with urinary/flank features. Obtain urine culture, assess sepsis, pregnancy, renal function and obstruction risk, choose empiric therapy from current local resistance guidance, and urgently decompress an infected obstructed system.
recognize: Fever, flank pain/CVA tenderness, nausea/vomiting and urinary symptoms are common but older/immunocompromised patients may present atypically.
Obstruction from stone or anatomic disease turns infection into a source-control emergency.
differentiate: Renal colic without infection can cause flank pain/hematuria but not the same septic syndrome.
assessment: Assess vitals/perfusion, pregnancy, vomiting/oral tolerance, immunocompromise, stones/obstruction, prior resistant organisms and renal function.
workup: Obtain urinalysis and urine culture; use CBC/chemistry/blood cultures/imaging based on severity and obstruction/abscess concern.
Routine imaging is not required for every uncomplicated responding case.
management: Use appropriate empiric antibiotics then narrow to culture/susceptibility.
Admit/IV therapy when septic, pregnant with significant illness, unable to tolerate oral therapy or otherwise high risk.
Urgently arrange decompression when infected obstruction is suspected.
medicationSafety: Dose-adjust renally cleared antibiotics and avoid nephrotoxic combinations when possible.
Do not rely on nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin-type lower-tract agents for renal parenchymal infection.
counselling: Teach completion/adherence and urgent return for worsening fever, vomiting, syncope or reduced urine output.
followUp: Review culture and clinical response; investigate recurrent/atypical disease for structural risk.
examTrap: Treating febrile flank-pain pyelonephritis with an antibiotic that only achieves lower urinary concentrations.
oneLinePearl: Pyelonephritis needs kidney-penetrating treatment—and obstruction needs drainage.

title: Nephrolithiasis: Relieve the Obstruction Risk, Then Prevent the Next Stone
bottomLine: Renal colic is usually managed conservatively when the patient is stable and the stone is likely to pass, but infection plus obstruction, solitary-kidney obstruction, AKI, uncontrolled pain/vomiting or other high-risk anatomy needs urgent urologic care. Recurrent stone prevention is based on stone type, hydration, diet and metabolic evaluation—not a blanket calcium-restriction diet.
recognize: Colicky flank pain radiating to groin, hematuria, nausea/vomiting are typical.
Fever is not routine uncomplicated renal colic and raises infected obstruction concern.
differentiate: AAA, ectopic pregnancy, pyelonephritis and other abdominal pathology can mimic renal colic.
Uric acid, calcium oxalate, struvite and cystine stones have different prevention strategies.
assessment: Assess fever/sepsis, urine output, renal function, solitary kidney, pregnancy, prior stones, diet, medications and pain/vomiting severity.
workup: Use urinalysis, renal function and imaging matched to pregnancy/radiation risk and local pathway; noncontrast CT is highly sensitive in many adults while ultrasound is preferred first in pregnancy/selected settings.
Recurrent/high-risk stones warrant stone analysis and metabolic evaluation.
management: Provide analgesia/antiemetics and hydration to euvolemia; use medical expulsive therapy selectively based on stone location/size and current urology guidance.
Prevent recurrence with high fluid intake, normal dietary calcium, sodium moderation and stone-specific therapy.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs are effective renal-colic analgesics but may be unsuitable with AKI, CKD, pregnancy or GI risk.
Do not advise severe dietary calcium restriction for common calcium stones because it can increase oxalate absorption.
counselling: Teach hydration and stone-straining/analysis when appropriate and prevention based on the actual stone phenotype.
followUp: Confirm passage/resolution when clinically required and arrange recurrent-stone metabolic/urology follow-up.
examTrap: Sending home a febrile obstructed stone as uncomplicated renal colic.
oneLinePearl: A stone plus infection is a drainage emergency.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association nephrolithiasis educational/guideline resources

title: Glomerulonephritis: Read the Sediment and Recognize Rapidly Progressive Disease
bottomLine: Glomerulonephritis is suggested by hematuria with glomerular sediment, proteinuria, hypertension, edema and declining kidney function. Rapidly rising creatinine, RBC casts/dysmorphic RBCs or systemic vasculitic features require urgent nephrology evaluation because kidney loss can become irreversible while the precise immune diagnosis is still being established.
recognize: Nephritic physiology includes hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, edema and AKI.
Pulmonary hemorrhage, purpura, sinus disease, neuropathy, arthritis or infection can point toward a systemic cause.
differentiate: Lower-tract hematuria generally lacks glomerular casts/proteinuria and renal dysfunction.
Nephrotic syndrome is dominated by heavy proteinuria/hypoalbuminemia/edema, though overlap occurs.
assessment: Assess BP/volume, urine output, systemic autoimmune/vasculitic symptoms, recent infection, medications and pulmonary symptoms.
workup: Use creatinine/electrolytes, urine ACR/protein, microscopy and cause-directed complement/ANA/ANCA/anti-GBM/infectious testing; renal biopsy is specialist-directed when diagnosis/prognosis will change treatment.
management: Urgently refer rapidly progressive disease and treat life-threatening hypertension, pulmonary edema, hyperkalemia or pulmonary hemorrhage in acute care.
Immunosuppression is disease-specific and should not begin blindly before infection/diagnosis considerations except under urgent specialist direction.
medicationSafety: Avoid nephrotoxins and dose-adjust medications during AKI.
Immunosuppressive regimens require infection screening/prophylaxis and agent-specific monitoring.
counselling: Explain why urgent specialist testing/biopsy may be needed even before symptoms become severe.
followUp: Track kidney function/proteinuria and ensure biopsy/serology results are acted upon.
examTrap: Treating hematuria plus rapidly rising creatinine as a simple UTI without examining the urinary sediment/proteinuria pattern.
oneLinePearl: Active sediment plus falling kidney function is glomerular disease until proven otherwise.
